title: India's 'Cockroach' Youth Protests Erupt Into Biggest Challenge to Modi in a Decade
excerpt: Tens of thousands of young Indians are demanding education reforms and the resignation of the education minister after NEET exam paper leaks affected 2 million students. Police tear gas and baton charges have only hardened their resolve.
body:
• The Cockroach Janta Party's "Chalo Sansad" march on July 20 turned into the largest protests New Delhi has seen in years, with police responding with tear gas, baton charges, and an internet shutdown.
  • Over 150 protesters were hospitalized after Monday's clashes; protests have since spread to Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, and at least five other cities across India.
  • Opposition leaders forced a suspension of parliament proceedings on Wednesday, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET paper leak that affected 2 million students.
  • The government has offered talks and a parliamentary debate, but protesters say they will not leave until their demands — including Pradhan's ouster and compensation for families of students who died by suicide — are met.

Thousands of young Indians remained camped at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Wednesday, two days after their march on parliament descended into the worst street violence India's capital has witnessed in years. The confrontation has grown into the most serious youth-led challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he took power in 2014.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a movement that began as online satire in May, organized a "Chalo Sansad" (March to Parliament) rally on Monday — the opening day of the Monsoon Session. Tens of thousands of mostly Gen-Z protesters attempted to reach the parliament complex, but were met with tear gas, baton charges, and water cannons. Delhi Police, which had imposed prohibitory orders and declared the march unlawful, said 180 people were injured, including 118 security personnel and 60 protesters. CJP leaders put the number of hospitalized protesters above 150.

The government also ordered an internet shutdown in central Delhi, a move that delayed but ultimately amplified the reach of videos showing the crackdown. The footage has since gone viral, sparking outrage across the country and internationally.

From Satire to Political Force

The CJP was founded by Boston University graduate Abhijeet Dipke after India's Chief Justice made comments widely interpreted as calling unemployed youth "cockroaches." Supporters embraced the insult, building a satirical movement that amassed millions of Instagram followers within days. But the satire hardened into genuine political mobilization after the leak of NEET UG 2026 question papers in May forced approximately 2 million medical school aspirants to re-sit the exam.

"What we face when you prepare for the whole year and at D-Day you hear it's rigged."

— Sudhir Kumar, protester and medical school aspirant

About a dozen students have died by suicide after the leak, according to media reports, unable to face sitting the exam again. The deaths galvanized the movement and sharpened its demands: the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, systemic exam reform, compensation of ₹1 crore ($104,000) for each bereaved family, and the release of activist Sonam Wangchuk, who began a hunger strike on June 28 in support of the students.

Crackdown and Defiance

On Monday evening, police demolished the makeshift protest camp at Jantar Mantar. By Tuesday morning, protesters had rebuilt it. Many returned bearing visible injuries — bruised faces, bandaged arms, torn clothing — and a sharpened resolve.

"But just in a flash, I don't know what happened, the police started hitting us with batons. Kids, women, old men, they hit everyone," Mohammad Taj, a protester from Haryana whose face was badly bruised, told CNN.

Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, one of Delhi's most prominent Sikh temples, opened its doors to hundreds of young protesters seeking shelter after the crackdown. "Everyone is welcome here. The common area and langar are open to everybody," said Paramjit Singh Chandhok, Chief Advisor to the Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee.

Political Fallout Intensifies

The protests have rapidly taken on a broader political dimension. On Tuesday, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and several senior party leaders staged a sit-in outside Modi's residence demanding Pradhan's removal. They were detained by police after refusing to leave, though released later that evening.

Gandhi issued a list of five demands, including the resignations of both Pradhan and Home Minister Amit Shah, action against police who assaulted students, withdrawal of cases filed against protesters, and a formal apology from the Prime Minister.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers — many dressed in black and carrying placards reading "Our children's future is not for sale" — forced a suspension of proceedings in both houses of parliament. They demanded a debate on alleged police brutality and the exam leak before any legislative business could proceed.

Government Responds, but Stops Short

Health Minister JP Nadda, who met CJP leaders on Monday, has urged protesters to end their sit-in while offering a parliamentary discussion on NEET. Pradhan, breaking his silence on Tuesday, said the governmentnment remained "100% committed to discussing NEET and addressing every genuine concern of our youth on the floor of the House."

"Student-led protests risk spiralling into a larger political and social challenge for the Modi government, as it has touched a raw nerve among a young, growing workforce that is struggling to find jobs."

— Shumita Deveshwar, chief India economist, TS Lombard

But neither Modi nor the BJP leadership has responded to calls for Pradhan's resignation, which analysts say signals the education minister's importance within the party hierarchy. Modi himself has vowed to punish those behind the leaks but has not addressed the protesters directly.

Protests Spread Nationwide

The movement has expanded well beyond Delhi. Demonstrations have erupted in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Goa, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram, Jammu, and Ahmedabad. In Chennai, students and activists were detained during protests, while rival demonstrations by Congress and BJP workers led to further detentions in Bengaluru.

Delhi Metro shut 16 stations in central areas on Wednesday due to security concerns, and more than 1,000 protesters remained at Jantar Mantar, waving Indian flags and chanting slogans in the rain. CJP leaders were reportedly due to hold a second round of talks with the government.

Meanwhile, Wangchuk — the Ladakhi education reformer who inspired the film "3 Idiots" — was moved to a private hospital on Tuesday after a court order, following a petition from his wife alleging he had been illegally detained by police when they forcibly removed him from the protest site over the weekend.

What Comes Next

The CJP's leaders have said they will not leave Jantar Mantar until their demands are met. With the Monsoon Session of parliament underway and opposition parties eager to corner the government, the pressure on Modi is unlikely to ease. Rahul Gandhi has called India's education system "rigged," alleging 152 paper leaks in 10 years with zero convictions.

For the millions of young Indians who see competitive exams as their only pathway to a middle-class life, the stakes could not be higher. The question now is whether the government's offer of parliamentary debate will be enough to defuse a movement that has already outgrown its satirical origins — and whether Modi, who has rarely faced sustained street pressure during his tenure, can afford to ignore it.
